name: Cologne / perfume

lead: Perfume is a blend of aroma compounds, fixatives and a solvent, usually ethanol, worn on skin or clothing. 'Cologne' originally meant the citrus-based eau de Cologne first sold in Cologne, Germany in 1709, and in American English it now usually means a men's fragrance.

On looksmaxxing forums fragrance is treated as a low-effort add-on to grooming, with members ranking popular bottles and debating whether scent matters if the face does not. No study in the sources reviewed tests whether wearing cologne changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: Fragrances evaporate in stages, with top notes disappearing first and base notes lasting longest. The strength of the formulation changes how long it lasts: Wikipedia lists parfum at about 15-30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum at 15-20%, eau de toilette at 5-15% and eau de cologne at 2-3%, with brands varying [2]. The scent is smelled by others; any effect on social impressions is not established by trial data.

Fragrance ingredients can cause contact dermatitis, headaches or asthma symptoms in sensitive people, and patch testing with fragrance mix gives a positive reaction in about 10% of people with eczema, according to Wikipedia [3]. A 2020 review of essential oils, which are common in fragrance, also describes adverse effects including endocrine-disrupting properties for some oils [5].

lead: Perfume is a mixture of fragrant essential oils or aroma compounds, fixatives and solvents, usually in liquid form. Fine fragrance typically uses ethanol or an ethanol-water mix as the solvent [1]. Products are classed by concentration, from parfum or extrait at about 15-30% down through eau de parfum, eau de toilette and eau de cologne at about 2-3%, though the terms are imprecise and brands differ [1].

Eau de Cologne ('water from Cologne') began as a citrus-based fragrance launched in Cologne, Germany in 1709 by the Italian perfumer Giovanni Maria Farina; the name later became a generic term for lightly concentrated scented waters of about 2-5% concentration [2]. In American English, 'cologne' usually refers to a men's fragrance, even when the product is an eau de toilette or eau de parfum [2].

Looksmaxxing forums place fragrance among grooming and 'style' tools. A looksmax.org thread ranks popular men's bottles by price and states that colognes 'only work' if a person is already good-looking [3]. No study in the sources reviewed tests whether wearing cologne improves perceived attractiveness, and published research relevant to fragrance concerns allergy and the health effects of ingredients [4][5].

paras: A fragrance is described by top, middle (heart) and base notes: top notes evaporate first and base notes last longest [1]. Wikipedia lists parfum or extrait at roughly 15-30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum at 15-20% (now the most common strength), eau de toilette at 5-15% (common for men's fragrances), eau de cologne at 2-3% and eau fraiche at 3% or less [1]. The article cautions that the terms are imprecise and that a product name at different strengths can use different formulations [1].

Traditional eau de Cologne uses dilute ethanol (70-90%) as a base with citrus oils such as lemon, bergamot and neroli [2]. Ingredients come from plants, from synthetic aroma compounds (such as musks) and, historically, from animal sources like ambergris, civet and musk, now largely replaced by synthetics [1].

Perfumery began in ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus Valley, and a Mesopotamian perfume maker named Tapputi appears on a second-millennium BC cuneiform tablet [1]. The 9th-century scholar Al-Kindi described many perfume recipes and Ibn Sina (Avicenna) popularised distillation for flower oils [1]. Giovanni Maria Farina launched the original eau de Cologne in Cologne in 1709 and it was supplied to many royal houses; after free trade under French control began in 1797 many other firms sold products under the same name, and the 4711 brand has been produced in Cologne since at least 1799 [2]. Modern perfumery began in the late 19th century with synthetic compounds such as vanillin and coumarin, and Guerlain's Jicky (1889) is noted as an early modern perfume [1].

Wikipedia states that adverse reactions to fragrance can include allergic contact dermatitis, asthma attacks and headaches, with contact dermatitis the most common allergic reaction [4]. Patch tests with fragrance mix give a positive result in about 10% of eczema patients, and an estimated 1.7-4.1% of the general population is sensitised to fragrance mix ingredients, a figure the article marks as needing a citation [4]. About 2,500 fragrance ingredients are used in consumer products, of which roughly 100 are known to cause reactions in some people [4].

A 2020 review in the Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine on essential oils, which are used in cologne among many products, summarises reported antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and mood-related properties as well as risks, including endocrine-disrupting effects for certain oils [5].

On looksmax.org, one member posted a ranked list of ten men's fragrances with approximate prices, from mid-range designer bottles to niche and luxury ones, and prefaced it by saying colognes only work for people who are already good-looking [3]. Another thread has a member describing plans to start a fragrance company [6].

Traditional advice summarised by Wikipedia is to apply fragrance to pulse points warmed by the body, to layer lighter products by day and stronger ones in the evening, and to expect that diet, medication and skin dryness can change how a scent performs [1].

No studies found on cologne or perfume for improving attractiveness. Research on related topics concerns fragrance allergy [4] and the health effects of essential oils, which are common fragrance ingredients [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org fragrance is a side topic: members post ranked lists of popular bottles and frame scent as an add-on to appearance rather than a replacement for it [3].
